title: Spring Boot: jobs, health checks and secrets
description: Scheduled and background jobs, ShedLock for multi-instance runs, @Async, Actuator health and Kubernetes probes, retries and secrets handling.
source: Spring Framework scheduling documentation; Spring Boot reference (task execution and scheduling, Actuator, Kubernetes probes, sanitising endpoints); Spring Framework 7 resilience documentation (@Retryable); ShedLock README; Kubernetes probe documentation
seriesTitle: Interview roadmap: Java and Spring Boot
seriesDescription: Java and Spring Boot interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Java/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Java only: nothing here mixes in Python.

questions.prompt: @Scheduled(cron = "0 0/15 * * * *") uses Spring's six-field cron (second minute hour day month weekday). How many times per hour does the method fire?
questions.explanation: Seconds=0, minutes=0/15 means minutes 0, 15, 30, 45 of every hour: 4 runs. Spring cron has a leading seconds field, unlike Unix cron.

questions.prompt: A Spring method is annotated @Scheduled(cron = "0 30 9 * * MON-FRI") (six fields: second minute hour day month weekday). How many times does it fire in four full weeks?
questions.explanation: It fires at 09:30:00 on each weekday: 5 per week x 4 weeks = 20. Remember the leading seconds field that Unix cron does not have.

questions.prompt: A @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 2000) method takes 3 seconds per run, and the first run starts at t = 0 s. There is a single scheduler thread. How many runs have started by t = 62 s, counting the one at t = 0?
questions.explanation: fixedDelay counts from the end of one run to the start of the next, so each cycle is 3 + 2 = 5 s and runs start at 0, 5, 10 ... 60: 13 starts. fixedRate = 2000 on one thread would instead start the next run as soon as the previous ends, never overlapping, because the default scheduler has one thread.

questions.prompt: A Spring app with a nightly @Scheduled cleanup job is deployed as 3 identical replicas and nothing coordinates them. How many times does the cleanup run each night across the cluster?
questions.explanation: Each instance has its own scheduler, so the job runs 3 times. Fixes: a distributed lock (ShedLock, Redis SET NX, DB advisory lock), a leader election, or a dedicated scheduler instance or Kubernetes CronJob.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring method cleanup() that runs at 02:00 every night (cron "0 0 2 * * *") and is protected by ShedLock: lock name "nightlyCleanup", held at most 10 minutes (ISO-8601 duration) so a crashed node cannot block it forever.
questions.explanation: ShedLock stores the lock in a shared database or Redis table; the first node to insert or update the row runs the job. lockAtLeastFor keeps a fast job from being re-run by a node whose clock is slightly ahead.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A @Async method called from another method of the same class runs synchronously on the caller's thread.
questions.reason: The async behaviour is applied by a proxy, and an internal this.call() bypasses that proxy.

whys.a: Correct: no proxy, no executor hand-off.

questions.explanation: Put async methods on another bean, and remember @EnableAsync. Same pitfall as @Transactional and @Cacheable.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring service method sendEmail(String to) that runs on a separate thread through Spring's async support and returns a CompletableFuture<Void> that is already completed once the work is done (call mail.send(to) first).
questions.explanation: The caller must reach the method through the proxy (another bean), and @EnableAsync must be present. Configure a bounded ThreadPoolTaskExecutor; the default executor settings are rarely right for production.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Spring's @Scheduled tasks run on a pool of 10 threads by default.
questions.reason: A @Scheduled method must take no arguments.

whys.d: Correct: the default scheduler is single-threaded (Boot's spring.task.scheduling.pool.size defaults to 1); R is true because the method must be void-compatible and argument-free.

questions.explanation: One slow job can delay all others. Set spring.task.scheduling.pool.size or use your own TaskScheduler.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: With the default single-thread scheduler, a @Scheduled(fixedRate = 1000) method that takes 3 seconds never runs concurrently with itself.
questions.reason: Boot's default scheduler uses a pool of 10 threads.

whys.a: Wrong: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because a single thread cannot start a second run while the first is busy, so runs start late; R is false because the default pool size is 1.

questions.explanation: Late runs queue up and start back to back. Raise spring.task.scheduling.pool.size if independent jobs must not delay each other, and guard against overlap explicitly if you do.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring Boot Actuator health indicator bean PaymentsHealth for a boolean method gateway.ping(): report UP when true, otherwise DOWN with the detail "gateway" set to "unreachable".
questions.explanation: A bean named PaymentsHealth appears as payments in /actuator/health. Beware: adding a flaky dependency to the aggregate health can mark the whole app DOWN.

questions.prompt: Match each probe or endpoint with what it means in Kubernetes / Spring Boot.

right.text: The pod is removed from Service endpoints but is not restarted
Other probes wait until a slow boot has finished

questions.explanation: Spring Boot exposes /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness probe groups (enabled automatically on Kubernetes, or via management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled).

questions.prompt: Your service depends on a database. Where should the DB check live to avoid a restart storm during a DB outage?

options.text: In readiness only; liveness should reflect only that the process itself is healthy.
options.why: Readiness failure stops traffic without killing pods.

options.text: In the liveness probe, so that pods that cannot reach the database are restarted quickly.
options.why: A DB outage would restart every pod and extend recovery.

options.text: In both probes with the same timeout.
options.why: This still triggers restarts of healthy processes.

options.text: In neither; health checks must never touch dependencies.
options.why: Readiness checks on critical dependencies are standard.

questions.explanation: Spring Boot's readiness group excludes external systems by default and liveness is for unrecoverable internal states.

questions.prompt: Complete the Kubernetes and Actuator probe vocabulary.
questions.text: A pod whose {1} probe fails is restarted by the kubelet; a pod whose {2} probe fails keeps running but receives no traffic. Spring Boot publishes both as health groups under /actuator/health.
questions.explanation: Boot enables the probe groups automatically on Kubernetes, or with management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true. During graceful shutdown the readiness state flips so the load balancer stops sending traffic first.

questions.prompt: A Spring Framework 7 bean method is annotated with plain @Retryable (no attributes, resilience support enabled) and always throws IOException. A caller invokes it once. How many times is the method body executed in total?
questions.explanation: Spring Framework 7's own @Retryable defaults to maxRetries = 3, which counts retries on top of the first call: 1 + 3 = 4 executions, with a 1 s delay. includes and excludes are empty, so every exception is retried. The older spring-retry library differs: its maxAttempts = 3 counts total attempts, and it uses retryFor (formerly include).

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are sound practices for configuration and secrets in a Spring Boot service?

options.text: Inject passwords through environment variables or a secrets manager.
options.why: Keeps secrets out of the repository and the image.

options.text: Commit application-prod.yml with the production database password.
options.why: Anything in git history must be treated as compromised.

options.text: Use @ConfigurationProperties with @Validated to fail fast on missing config.
options.why: Binding validation stops the application at startup rather than at first use.

options.text: Log every property at startup to simplify debugging.
options.why: That writes secrets into log aggregation.

options.text: Leave Actuator's env and configprops values masked, which is the default in current Boot versions.
options.why: The show-values property defaults to NEVER, so values are hidden unless you opt in.

options.text: Bake the payment API key into the Docker image.
options.why: Anyone who can pull the image can read the key.

questions.explanation: Principle: config in the environment (twelve-factor), secrets from a vault, validate at boot, never log them.
